result:
Marginalia is my favorite genre of writing, and almost none of it was meant to be read.

The most famous example is Fermat's. Around 1637 he scribbled in his copy of Diophantus that he had a marvelous proof of a theorem, which the margin was too narrow to contain. Mathematicians spent the next 358 years trying to find it. He probably didn't have one, which means the most productive sentence in the history of mathematics may have been a mistake, written to nobody.

Coleridge wrote so well in margins that friends lent him books hoping he would deface them. Charles Lamb said the books came back "enriched with annotations, tripling their value."

But I like the anonymous ones best. A "NO" in block capitals beside a confident paragraph. An exclamation mark pressed hard enough to dent the next page. "Ha" next to a joke two hundred years old. These are records of a mind caught in the act of reacting, before it had time to arrange itself into an opinion. Published criticism tells you what someone decided to think. A margin tells you what happened to them on page 112.

The author speaks first, at length, and the reader answers in a cramped space with a dull pencil, knowing the author will never hear it. People do it anyway. Medieval scribes did it too, complaining in the borders of manuscripts about cold hands and thin ink.

Given half an inch of blank space, people talk back.
